processing: A needle-shaped green made from tender young material; the details of its firing are little documented, though it is shaped straight and tight like other needle greens.
harvest_season: Spring, as is usual for bud-grade Zhejiang greens; the earliest pickings are the most valued.
appearance_dry: Straight, sword-like needles with down over a jade green, even and upright.
appearance_wet: Tender shoots of a soft jade green, standing much like lotus hearts.
taste_profile: A clean fragrance with a sweet, soft finish, in keeping with its light bud-heavy material.

brewing.notes: Use a tall glass to watch the needles. Bud-heavy greens scald easily, so let the water cool first.

vintage_note: Usual for Zhejiang bud-grade greens: sold as the current spring's harvest, with the earliest picking priced highest, and best within the year. It has no ageing tradition. Specific grades and seasons for this tea are little documented.
description:
Xueshui Yunlü, 'snow-water cloud green', is a needle-shaped green from the hills of Tonglu county in Hangzhou. It counts among the handful of named local teas around the city, alongside Jingshan and Tianmu Qingding, and sits well outside the shadow of West Lake Long Jing in looks.

Its identity is its shape: straight needles likened to a drawn silver sword, or to a lotus heart, with jade colour showing through the down. That points to very tender material, and it is a major part of how the tea is judged.

The cup is described as bright tender green, clean in fragrance and sweet. As with other bud-heavy greens, cooler water and a clear glass show it at its best and keep it from turning flat or sharp.

Little is documented about grades, so judge it as you would any needle green: even shape, fresh smell, and a harvest date from this spring.
history:
Its history is thinly documented. Chinese references present it as a modern famous tea credited with helping to open the way for needle-shaped teas in Zhejiang, and mention gold awards at national and international tea competitions, but give little on who created it or when.

It is now named among Hangzhou's regional teas, with Tonglu as its home.
